title: Ful Medames
subtitle: Egyptian slow-cooked broad beans with lemon and cumin
excerpt: Egypt's national dish and the breakfast of millions: dried broad beans simmered until very soft, then mashed and dressed with olive oil, lemon, cumin, and garlic. Eaten with boiled eggs, raw vegetables, and flatbread for dipping.

recipe.sourceNotes: Ful medames (the name means cooked or buried beans, a reference to the ancient method of burying the clay pot in embers overnight) is Egypt's national dish and one of the oldest continuously eaten foods on Earth, documented since Pharaonic times. It is eaten for breakfast across Egypt and throughout the Arab world, cooked from the previous evening in a special long-necked copper pot called a damasa that keeps the beans warm overnight. The dish has spread across the Middle East and North Africa with countless regional variations: in Lebanon it is eaten with tomatoes; in Sudan with sesame oil and chilli; in Ethiopia as the base for ful. The essential form is always the same: slow-cooked broad beans, olive oil, lemon, and cumin. Tinned broad beans can be used to shorten cooking considerably.

content.text: If using dried beans, soak them overnight and allow 90 minutes to 2 hours of simmering time. Tinned broad beans (or tinned fava beans) are a quicker substitute and produce a good result with 20 minutes of cooking. The beans should be soft enough to mash easily with the back of a spoon; do not leave them with any firmness. Dress generously with olive oil just before serving.

items.preparation: tinned fava/broad beans, drained and rinsed; or 200 g dried, soaked overnight
2 crushed raw for dressing, 2 added to cooking water

content.text: If using dried beans, drain the soaked beans and cover with fresh water by 5 cm. Add 2 garlic cloves. Bring to the boil and simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours until very soft, adding boiling water as needed to keep the beans submerged. If using tinned beans, put them in a pan with their liquid and simmer for 20 minutes.

When the beans are very soft, remove from the heat. Mash roughly with the back of a spoon or a potato masher, leaving some texture. Add the crushed raw garlic, lemon juice, cumin, olive oil, and salt. Stir to combine. Add a little of the cooking water if the mixture is too thick; it should be the consistency of a loose dip.
Spoon into bowls and top with parsley, chilli flakes, and a generous pour of olive oil. Serve with halved hard-boiled eggs, diced tomato, and flatbread for scooping.
